summary: Provides a profile for tuning TCP over paths that include 2.5G and 3G wireless networks. It describes their relevant characteristics, recommends TCP algorithm choices for endpoints on such paths, and discusses open issues. It is a Best Current Practice.

plainLanguage.summary: Mobile networks have quirks like delays and brief outages. This note says which TCP settings work best when a connection crosses a cellular network.

questions: what tcp settings work best over 3g
what is the tcp initial window for wireless
should i use header compression on wireless tcp
why do delay spikes cause tcp timeouts
subtitle: A short list of safe, standard TCP settings that work well when a connection crosses a 2.5G or 3G cellular link.

tldr.problem: 2.5G and 3G wireless links have high latency, sudden delay spikes, changing data rates and handovers, which confuse TCP and cause slow starts, spurious timeouts and wasted transmissions.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC recommends one profile of existing standards-track TCP options for both generations: suitable window sizes, a larger initial window, Limited Transmit, bigger MTUs, Path MTU discovery, SACK, ECN and Timestamps, plus turning off RFC 1144 header compression.
tldr.outcome: It is a Best Current Practice that lists only mechanisms the community considers safe on the general Internet, and it sets aside experimental ideas as open issues.

facts.label: Typical RTT
facts.value: A few hundred milliseconds to one second

today: RFC 3481 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 71). According to the metadata for this site it has not been obsoleted or updated by another RFC. It describes 2.5G and 3G networks as they were in February 2003.

sections.title: Why a TCP Profile for 2.5G and 3G
sections.content:
Second-generation (2G) cellular systems mostly gave circuit-switched data at 10-20 kbps. 2.5G (for example GPRS) and 3G (for example Wideband CDMA and cdma2000) were introduced for higher data rates, and Internet access became a primary motivation.

This RFC proposes a profile: a set of TCP configuration options that work particularly well on 2.5G and 3G paths. All of them are commonly found in modern TCP stacks, and are standards-track mechanisms judged safe even on non-wireless paths. One set covers both generations because they pose similar challenges. The RFC gives two example users: WAP 2.0, which adopted TCP, and i-mode over FOMA, which uses the profile.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a short checklist of safe settings for phones on cell networks. The same list works for both older and newer cell networks.

sections.title: How 2.5G and 3G Links Behave
sections.content:
The RFC lists link traits that affect TCP.

  • Latency: typical round-trip time ranges from a few hundred milliseconds to one second.
  • Data rates: 2.5G has 10-20 kbps uplink and 10-40 kbps downlink; initial 3G is expected to be around 64 kbps uplink and 384 kbps downlink. The bandwidth-delay product is around 1-5 KB for 2.5G and 8-50 KB for 3G, so 2.5G links are Long Thin Networks and 3G links approach Long Fat Networks. Rates also change with other users and mobility.
  • Asymmetry: not more than 3-6 times, which TCP tolerates without ACK congestion control or ACK filtering, so those are out of scope.
  • Delay spikes: sudden delays of several times the typical RTT, caused by coverage loss, handovers, rerouting, high-priority traffic or scheduling. They can cause spurious timeouts and needless retransmissions.
  • Loss: link-level retransmission keeps IP packet loss low but shows up as delay jitter, lengthening the retransmission timeout.
  • Handovers and bandwidth oscillation: moving between 2.5G and 3G changes link properties, and features negotiated at connection setup cannot be changed later. Repeated allocation and release of high-speed channels is called bandwidth oscillation.
sections.plainLanguage: The phone road is slow to answer, it sometimes freezes for a moment, and its speed changes as you move or as other people join. TCP has to cope with all that.

sections.title: Example Radio Technologies
sections.content:
The RFC gives short tours of three technologies to show what link layers do, not to be complete.

GPRS and HSCSD extend GSM. HSCSD gives a user multiple timeslots on a fast circuit-switched link; GPRS is packet-switched, shares timeslots and is always on. Its RLC protocol provides ARQ over the radio link.

W-CDMA uses RLC, a selective-repeat sliding-window ARQ, with a 16-bit header; typically 336-bit PDUs are used, and one to twelve PDUs make up an FEC frame. The maximum number of retransmissions is configurable up to 40. To TCP, a 384 kbps radio bearer looks like a path with a bandwidth-delay product of up to 50 KB.

cdma2000 offers speeds up to 316.8 kbps in 1XRTT and 2 Mbps in 1X-EV. Its Radio Link Protocol is NAK-based: the receiver does not acknowledge good frames, it sends NAKs in rounds for missing ones, and may fail to recover some.
sections.plainLanguage: Different phone networks fix lost pieces in their own ways, by asking for missing pieces again. That fixing takes time, so TCP sees delays instead of losses.

sections.title: Window, Initial Window, Limited Transmit and MTU
sections.content:
The recommendations are for the data sender, the data receiver, or both. The first four concern sizing and early behavior.

  • Window size: pick windows based on the bandwidth-delay product. The TCP specification limits the receiver window to 64 KB, so use the window scale option above that; default buffers of around 16 KB should be increased.
  • Increased initial window: TCP over 2.5G/3G SHOULD set the initial congestion window to min (4*MSS, max (2*MSS, 4380 bytes)), which is two to four segments and roughly 4 KB. It matters most for transfers of a few segments.
  • Limited Transmit (RFC 3042): implementations SHOULD implement it, so small windows can still trigger Fast Retransmit instead of waiting for a timeout.
  • IP MTU larger than default: designers may choose from small values such as 576 bytes up to link limits such as 1500 bytes, and are encouraged to choose larger ones. This applies to 3G; on 2.5G use caution as in RFC 3150.
sections.plainLanguage: Use a big enough box for packages in flight, start by sending a few packages instead of one, and use bigger boxes if the road can handle them.

sections.title: Loss Recovery, Timestamps and Header Compression
sections.content:
The remaining recommendations deal with detecting congestion and loss, and timing.

  • Path MTU discovery (RFC 1191 and RFC 1981 for IPv6): implementations should implement it, and routers must generate the needed ICMP messages.
  • SACK (RFC 2018): TCP SHOULD support it. Without SACK, use NewReno (RFC 2582).
  • ECN (RFC 3168): TCP SHOULD support it, but benefits appear only when ECN-capable routers are on the path.
  • Timestamps option: TCP SHOULD use it. It lets the sender sample RTT from every acknowledged segment and so avoid spurious timeouts when delay spikes occur. The cost is 12 bytes of overhead (4% at an MTU of 296 bytes, 0.8% at 1500 bytes) and it defeats RFC 1144 compression.
  • Disable RFC 1144 header compression: it performs badly with packet loss, because a lost segment desynchronizes the compressor and decompressor and the receiver discards the rest of the window. It SHOULD NOT be enabled unless loss between compressor and decompressor is very low.
sections.plainLanguage: Use ways to tell the sender exactly which pieces were lost, mark the road when it is crowded, and time the replies more carefully. Skip a trick that breaks when a piece is lost.

sections.title: Open Issues
sections.content:
Apart from the initial RTO discussion, the mechanisms in this section are not part of any standards-track RFC at the time of writing, so they cannot be recommended for the Internet in general.

  • Better header compression that handles SYN, FIN and TCP options.
  • Active queue management (RFC 2309), which reduces stale queued data and the risk of a spurious timeout for the first segment.
  • Avoiding extra round trips, though T/TCP was not adopted because of security concerns.
  • Making TCP robust against spurious timeouts, reordering and duplication.
  • The initial RTO: the standard says not below 3 seconds, which may be too low at bit rates as low as about 10 kb/s, so a larger value may be advisable. Experiments suggest following all of RFC 2988, including a minimum RTO of 1 second and restarting the timer when an ACK arrives, reduces spurious retransmissions.
sections.plainLanguage: There are more ideas that might help, but they are still being tested, so the note only mentions them as things to watch.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security section is brief. In 2.5G/3G networks, data is ciphertext over the air but cleartext between the Radio Access Network and the core network. Users can deploy IP security or TLS on their devices for end-to-end protection.

The RFC makes no IANA requests: it says the specification requires no IANA actions.
sections.plainLanguage: Messages are scrambled while flying through the air but not on the wires behind the tower, so people who need real secrecy should scramble their own messages.
